idiom_name: sealed interface Shape permits ... + exhaustive switch over both operands
implementation_notes: Since Java 21 the compiler proves coverage over a sealed hierarchy, so a pattern switch replaces the classic visitor for hierarchies you own: switch on the first operand and nest a switch (or match a record Pair with record patterns) on the second, and javac rejects the build when a permitted type is unhandled. That removes accept methods and visitor classes while keeping the compile-time guarantee the visitor provided. Two independent open hierarchies still need the classic visitor (see classic-visitor), because pattern switches are only exhaustive when the selector type is sealed and you cannot seal someone else's classes.
pitfalls: A default arm re-hides the exhaustiveness check: with sealed types, the switch without default is the whole point.
An exhaustive switch can still throw MatchException at runtime if the sealed hierarchy was recompiled without recompiling the switch: migrate and recompile together.
Nested switches repeat the outer arms: factor the pair into a record and use record patterns once the matrix grows.

variants.name: Visitor interface + accept() (classic double dispatch)
variants.idiom_name: ShapeVisitor with one visit overload per element + accept(ShapeVisitor)
variants.implementation_notes: The canonical Java realization: Shape declares accept(ShapeVisitor), every element implements it as v.visit(this), and the visitor declares one overload per concrete element type, so adding an element type stops the build everywhere it matters. It remains the answer for open hierarchies, for element classes from a library, and for every Java version before 21 - javac's own tree visitor API is this structure. Overload resolution works because inside Circle.accept the expression this has static type Circle, which is exactly the trick that makes the pair known.
pitfalls: An overload visit(Shape) silently absorbs new element types: its deliberate absence is the compile-time check.
A visitor that stores partial results is single-use; reusing it returns the previous traversal's state.
Adding a method to the visitor interface breaks every external implementation - use a default method only if the semantics are genuinely optional.
